Chapter One · The Personal Chronicle

THE MAN BEHIND
THE SCREEN

A life shaped by curiosity, music, friendship, machines, mountains, and the things I am still becoming.

“I was never the most talented kid in the room. I was simply curious enough to keep trying.”

My name is Mohammad Sakib Miya. I was born on March 18, 2008, in Syangja, Nepal. My village is Ghate, and it is where my story began. My childhood was ordinary in many ways: I was a middle-of-the-pack student, not exceptionally talented and not the least capable either. I played, explored, made mistakes, and slowly discovered what made me excited about life.

I started my education at a local Montessori and later studied at Jyoti English Secondary Boarding School in Syangja, where I completed my schooling and Grade 10 at the age of 16. After that, I moved to Pokhara for better educational opportunities and studied +2 at Gurukul Bidhya Sadan. I lived in a hostel, met new friends, experienced a different environment, and spent two memorable years full of laughter, new cultures, trips, and growing up. I completed my +2 studies in early 2083 BS.

  • BIRTHPLACE
    Syangja, Nepal
  • MY VILLAGE
    Ghate, Syangja
  • EDUCATION
    Jyoti School · Gurukul Bidhya Sadan
  • CURRENT CHAPTER
    Learning, building, exploring
  • PERSONAL MOTTO
    Keep learning. Keep moving.

THIS IS MY STORY. STILL IN PROGRESS.

01 / CHILDHOOD IN GHATE, SYANGJA

My story began in Ghate, with curiosity and small adventures.

I was born in Syangja, Nepal, and Ghate is my village. My story did not begin with expensive devices, a perfect plan, or a clear idea of what I wanted to become. It began with ordinary moments and a strong curiosity about what existed beyond the world around me. One of the places that caught my attention was a cybercafé near home. I would watch people playing GTA Vice City, fascinated by the open world, the cars, the missions, and the feeling that a screen could take you somewhere completely different.

My father once brought home a tablet, and for a while it felt like having a whole new world in my hands. When it broke, that little chapter ended. Later, I had a low-spec laptop that could not handle the biggest games, but it still gave me Paint, a few pre-installed games, and room to experiment. I learned to enjoy what I had instead of waiting for perfect equipment. Looking back, those early experiences connect many of my interests today: games, technology, design, machines, and the urge to figure out how things work.

02 / MOVING TO POKHARA & HOSTEL LIFE

Pokhara was a new city, a hostel, and a new chapter of growing up.

I studied at Jyoti English Secondary Boarding School in Syangja and passed Grade 10 at sixteen. After that, I moved to Pokhara for +2 at Gurukul Bidhya Sadan and lived in a hostel. It was a real change: a new city, a different routine, sharing space with other people, managing everyday responsibilities, and learning to live away from the familiar places and people I had grown up around.

Hostel life was not only about classes, homework, and exams. It was also conversations, jokes, friends, gaming, plans, small arguments, trips, and the ordinary moments that become important when you look back. Some people I met in Pokhara encouraged me to keep learning and take coding seriously. That support mattered because I was still figuring out what I was good at and what kind of future I wanted. My friends helped make the city feel less unfamiliar, and the experiences taught me that growing up often happens quietly, through daily life rather than one dramatic event.

I completed +2 in early 2083 BS. I do not see that as the end of my education; I see it as a point where I have to choose what to work toward next. I want to carry the good memories, the lessons, and the friendships with me, while also being honest that I am still learning how to plan, stay consistent, and make my ambitions real.

03 / GAMING, TECHNOLOGY, CARS & AVIATION

Games, computers, cars, and planes keep my curiosity alive.

During the COVID period, Minecraft and Free Fire became a big part of my life. There were days when gaming distracted me from online classes; at the time, it was easy to lose track of time inside a game. In Grade 10, my friends and I sometimes went to gaming houses to play GTA V and FIFA. When I reached Grade 11, my father bought me a better laptop, and I finally got to play more of the large, detailed games I had watched and wanted to try for years. Games were entertainment, but they also made me curious about environments, graphics, interfaces, and the technology behind the experience.

I started exploring coding around Grade 9. At first, I was not confident. Mathematics was difficult for me, and comments I heard at school made me question whether technology was the right direction. For a while, that doubt was louder than my curiosity. Moving to Pokhara changed things: friends encouraged me to keep learning, try ideas, and make things myself instead of deciding too early that I could not do it. I began returning to coding with a different mindset—progress did not have to happen all at once.

Today, I am working on web development and personal website projects, learning Python, and exploring tools such as NumPy, Pandas, Excel, and Power BI as I move toward data analysis and AI. I enjoy the process of taking an idea, breaking it into smaller problems, and turning it into something people can actually use. I am still learning and I know I have a long way to go, but I want my work to show that curiosity can become a skill when you keep practising.

I have always been drawn to machines: cars, racing cars, motorcycles, off-road SUVs, and the details that separate one vehicle from another. I like thinking about engines, horsepower, torque, mileage, handling, design, and what makes a vehicle suited to a particular road. A car is not just something that takes you from one place to another; to me, it is a mix of engineering, sound, performance, practicality, and personality. I can enjoy the look of a vehicle, then immediately want to know how it performs, how much fuel it uses, and how it would handle a long drive through the mountains.

My interest in aviation is just as personal. Aircraft used to pass over my childhood home, and whenever I heard or saw one, I would stop what I was doing and look up. That habit grew into a fascination with planes, helicopters, runways, airports, and the work that makes flight possible. I like the idea of the sky as a place full of engineering, precision, and possibility. Aviation and cars may be different worlds, but both make me curious about the people, systems, and machines behind them.

04 / MOUNTAINS, EVEREST & NIMS DAI

The mountains gave me a dream: one day, to stand on Everest.

There is something about mountains that I have never quite been able to explain. When I see them, I can keep looking for hours without getting bored. I do not always need to hike toward them or reach a summit; sometimes, simply standing there and watching is enough. The shape of the ridgelines, the way the light changes across the slopes, the clouds drifting past, and the sheer scale of them can hold my attention in a way that is difficult to put into words. It feels as if my mind grows quiet while my eyes keep searching the view, finding something new every time I look. I can be there for a long time and still feel that I have not seen enough. It is more than saying the mountains are beautiful. It is a feeling I recognise immediately, even if I cannot fully describe it.

My love for mountains grew as I watched climbers take on Everest around Grade 7 or 8. Seeing people face such a huge challenge made me imagine standing on that summit one day. That dream has stayed with me. I know Everest is not just a beautiful view or a simple adventure; it demands preparation, patience, courage, and respect for the mountain. But the thought of one day seeing that world with my own eyes continues to inspire me.

A friend later introduced me to 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible and Nirmal “Nims Dai” Purja, and his story gave my admiration for the mountains another meaning. What inspires me most is that he did not begin his mountaineering journey as a child who had spent his whole life climbing. He built a career in the Gurkhas and later served in the British military’s elite Special Boat Service. It was around the age of 29 or 30, in 2012, that a trek to Everest Base Camp changed the direction of his life. Along the trail, he saw Ama Dablam and became curious about what it would feel like to climb a mountain himself. That curiosity led him to climb Lobuche East—and a new chapter began.

He kept developing his mountaineering skills while still serving in the military. In 2014, he climbed Dhaulagiri, his first mountain above 8,000 metres, and in 2016 he reached the summit of Everest for the first time. Later, he left his military career to pursue an ambition that many people thought was impossible: climbing all fourteen of the world’s 8,000-metre peaks in a remarkably short period. In 2019, his Project Possible expedition achieved that goal in six months and six days. His journey reminds me that a dream does not have to begin early to become extraordinary. Sometimes it begins with one unexpected view, one question, and the courage to take the first step.

I had formed an opinion about him too quickly from things I saw online. Learning more about his journey reminded me that a person’s story is bigger than a few things seen out of context. It taught me to understand before judging—and it made the mountains feel even more connected to determination, humility, and the choices people make when they pursue something extraordinary. When I think about my own dream of Everest, I remember that there is no single age at which a passion must begin. I can keep looking at mountains for hours, wondering what lies beyond the ridges, and let that feeling guide me toward my own adventures.

05 / MUSIC, NEPATHYA & THE BANDS THAT SHAPED ME

From Hindi favourites to Nepali rock, folk, and the unforgettable Nepathya story.

Music has become one of the ways I remember places and people. Arijit Singh and Atif Aslam were part of my early listening, and I still return to their songs. Nepathya opened a different door for me: their concerts made me appreciate how Nepali music can connect generations and turn a crowd into one shared voice. The memories from Pokhara and Bandipur, and the unexpected meeting with Amrit Gurung on that rainy day, are now tied to the songs I heard around those moments. I am looking forward to Nepathya’s Syangja concert on Mangsir 6, which feels especially meaningful as I think about the next stage of my life.

My Nepali favourites reach well beyond one band. I listen to Nepathya, 1974 AD, Albatross, Anuprastha, Tribal Rain, The Elements, Monkey Temple, Night, Bipul Chettri, Pahelo Batti Muni, Diwas Gurung, Underside Nepal, and Ayurveda. Every artist brings a different sound and feeling, from rock and alternative music to folk-inspired songwriting. And I have to say it clearly: Night is the most underrated band I have ever seen. I think they deserve much more attention, and I want more people to discover them.

Bipul Chettri is another artist I admire. I thought I might have to miss his upcoming Pokhara performance because of some problems, but then I won a meet-and-greet pass. I am excited about the opportunity and the memory I hope to make. Outside Nepal, I love Pink Floyd, Metallica, AC/DC, Guns N’ Roses, John Denver, Queen, and Scorpions—with Scorpions among my favourite bands. These artists sound very different from one another, but that is what I enjoy: music for different moods, journeys, and stages of life.

In the end, music is not just a list of names on my profile. It is a concert with friends, a song that brings a place back to me, a band I discovered later than I wish I had, and the excitement of waiting for the next live performance. It belongs alongside the games I grew up with, the machines I love, the mountains I dream about, and the people who have shaped my life. This is the soundtrack I carry with me.

Nepathya ↗1974 AD ↗Albatross ↗Anuprastha ↗Tribal Rain ↗The Elements ↗Monkey Temple ↗Night — MOST UNDERRATED ↗Bipul Chettri ↗Pahelo Batti Muni ↗Diwas Gurung ↗Underside Nepal ↗Ayurveda ↗Pink Floyd ↗Metallica ↗AC/DC ↗Guns N’ Roses ↗John Denver ↗Queen ↗Scorpions ↗Arijit Singh ↗Atif Aslam ↗

For a long time, Hindi music was the centre of my playlist. I loved Arijit Singh and listened to Atif Aslam. Then I went to my first Nepathya concert in Pokhara. I knew songs like “Taal Ko Pani” and “Jogale Huncha Bhet,” but the concert changed how I heard the band. Seeing people of different ages singing and dancing together, and watching Amrit Gurung on stage, made me want to explore Nepali music more deeply. It was not just a performance; it was a room full of people sharing something that belonged to all of them.

Later, I travelled to Bandipur with friends for another Nepathya concert. I still remember the moment Niraj Nepathya began “Rama Rama” and Amrit appeared. The energy, the people, and being there with friends turned it into a memory I keep returning to. I tried to meet Amrit the following morning, but it did not happen. I met Jack Dai, a familiar podcaster, instead—and went home with the hope that maybe I would get another chance one day.

That chance came unexpectedly in Pokhara. My mother had just passed her driving-licence trial, and we had spent time waiting for the CCTV confirmation. After dropping her at Prithvi Chowk, I was caught in heavy rain near Sabhagriha Chowk and took shelter by a traditional clothing shop. I noticed an older man in a cap and round glasses, dressed in black and holding a black umbrella. I recognised him and asked, “Hajur Amrit Gurung ho ra?” He said yes. We took photos, but the first one was blurry because the camera lens was wet. He kindly helped me understand what was wrong. I remember the handshake, his eyes, and how calmly he treated me. Afterwards, I ran through New Road in the rain, smiling to myself. It was a small encounter, but it meant a lot to me.

My Nepali favourites include Nepathya, 1974 AD, Albatross, Anuprastha, Tribal Rain, The Elements, Monkey Temple, Night, Bipul Chettri, Pahelo Batti Muni, Diwas Gurung, Underside Nepal, and Ayurveda. Night is, to me, one of the most underrated bands I have seen, and I wish more people would discover them. Internationally, I listen to Pink Floyd, Metallica, AC/DC, Guns N’ Roses, John Denver, Queen, Scorpions, Arijit Singh, and Atif Aslam. Their sounds range from rock and alternative music to folk, classic songs, and emotional melodies—and each one belongs to a different part of my soundtrack.

06 / THE LIFE I AM WORKING TOWARD

I have big dreams, but I want to earn them one step at a time.

I am interested in a future where technology gives me the skills and freedom to build a life of my own. One path I am seriously considering is an IT-related Ausbildung in Germany: improving my German, strengthening my technical skills, gaining practical experience, and eventually building a stable career. I want to keep learning outside formal education too, especially in web development, Python, data analysis, and AI. I would love to create useful projects, build a portfolio that reflects my actual abilities, and work toward opportunities that once felt far away.

I also want to travel, take road trips, see more mountains, learn more about aviation, and experience places beyond Nepal. I want to keep making websites and creative projects, and perhaps build online work around technology or videos as I improve. These are ambitions, not promises that everything will happen exactly as imagined. I know there will be setbacks and decisions I have not figured out yet. What matters to me is staying curious, improving steadily, and not letting one difficult subject or one person’s opinion decide the limits of my future.

This website is part portfolio and part personal time capsule. It holds the things I make, the interests that keep me curious, and the memories I do not want to lose as life changes. I am proud of where I come from, grateful for the people who have encouraged me, and aware that I still have a lot to learn. I do not have the whole road mapped out. I am building the next part as I go.
